Johann Reuchlin
yō´hän roik´lĭn
n. (Johann Reuchlin, 1455–1522, German humanist and the first Christian Hebraist of rank, author of De Rudimentis Hebraicis, who defended the Jewish books against destruction)
German Reuchlin, a diminutive of Rauch, smoke; he sometimes Graecized himself as Capnion, from kapnos, smoke.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Johann Reuchlin gave the Western church the tools to read the Old Testament in Hebrew. His De Rudimentis Hebraicis of 1506 is a grammar and lexicon together, and he said of it, with justice, that he had raised a monument more lasting than bronze: every Protestant exegete of the next century learned from it or from books built on it, and Luther's Old Testament work was possible because of it. He then faced the test of his life. A converted Jew named Pfefferkorn, backed by the Cologne Dominicans, obtained an imperial order for the seizure and burning of Hebrew books; Reuchlin was asked for an opinion and gave it against the burning, arguing that the Talmud and the rabbinic commentaries should be studied, not destroyed, and that the Jews were fellow citizens with legal rights. The controversy consumed a decade and nearly ruined him. His ground is Rom 3:2, that to the Jews “were committed the oracles of God,” and Rom 11:1, “Hath God cast away his people? God forbid.” Rom 10:1 is the right affection toward them: Paul's “heart's desire and prayer to God for Israel is, that they might be saved.”

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines Hebrew as the language of the Hebrews; and an oracle, in Scripture, as the communications, revelations or messages delivered by God to prophets.

HE'BREW, n. A Hebrew; one of the descendants of Abraham. 2. The Hebrew language.

OR'ACLE, n. In Scripture, the communications, revelations or messages delivered by God to prophets.

2. The sanctuary, or most holy place in the temple.

Key Scripture

Rom 3:2 — "Much every way: chiefly, because that unto them were committed the oracles of God."

Rom 11:1 — "I say then, Hath God cast away his people? God forbid. For I also am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin."

Rom 10:1 — "Brethren, my heart's desire and prayer to God for Israel is, that they might be saved."

Deu 4:2 — "Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it, that ye may keep the commandments of the LORD your God which I command you."

Modern Corruption

Reuchlin stood against the burning of the Hebrew books, and the church that wanted them burned was proposing to destroy the language of its own Old Testament.

expand to see more

The proposal to burn the Jewish books was the fruit of a long and wicked tradition, and it was also self-defeating: a church that destroys Hebrew learning cannot read Moses. Reuchlin's defence rested on both grounds, the justice owed to his neighbours and the usefulness of the books to Christian scholarship, and Rom 3:2 is the deeper reason — the oracles of God were committed to this people, and the Christian who despises them despises the vessel of his own Scriptures. The medieval persecution of the Jews is to be named as sin, not explained as a product of its age.

Reuchlin's own weakness lay elsewhere. He was an enthusiast for the Kabbalah, believing that its mysteries confirmed Christian doctrine and that the divine names held hidden power, and he wrote two books arguing it. That is not Hebrew scholarship but occult speculation, and Deu 4:2 forbids the addition: what God has commanded is not supplemented by a secret tradition. The recovery is to take the grammar and leave the mysticism, and to hold toward the Jewish people the affection of Rom 10:1 rather than either the contempt of his opponents or the credulity of his own Kabbalism.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek logion (G3051), an oracle, a divine utterance; apoballo (G683 sense), to cast away; Hebrew dabar (H1697), word.

Usage

"“Hath God cast away his people? God forbid” (Rom 11:1) — against the burners."

"“my heart's desire and prayer to God for Israel is, that they might be saved” (Rom 10:1) — the right affection."
